Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz) for giving us an opportunity to discuss this subject. I wish that he, as an able medical doctor, had been consulted by the CBC in which case the corporation might not have included an irresponsible statement in its program on the subject last Monday.
This afternoon I tabled the most recent report of the National Advisory Committee on Immunizing Agents. These recommendations relate to the 1976-77 influenza immunization program, and I have accepted them in their entirety. They have been transmitted to the provincial ministers of health for their information and I have expressed my hope the provinces will look upon the committee's recommendations with favor.
It will be noted that the recommendations are substantially the same as those presented following the committee's meeting in June. The only essential differences are specific recommendations for the use of bivalent vaccine in children suffering from chronic neuromuscular disorders, cancer, and conditions involving biological defence mechanisms. While routine vaccination of school children is not recommended, special formulations of the vaccines are being prepared for those under twenty years of age with specific chronic illnesses. In reviewing its recommendations the committee endorsed the utilization of vaccine, both bivalent and monovalent, as supplies become available. The committee gave due consideration to alternatives to its recommended program, especially the question of stockpiling monovalent A/New Jersey vaccine and its utilization if further evidence of "swine influenza" activity became available.
The committee did not consider stockpiling to be a viable option for a variety of reasons: first, because influenza caused by a new virus spreads throughout the population with great rapidity and the possibility of receiving a sufficiently early warning by the isolation of virus from the first case is very remote. Secondly, laboratory identification of the virus takes a minimum of ten days and further time will elapse to investigate the case in order to ensure that it has been spread from person to person. A third important factor is that it has been estimated a minimum time lag of five to eight weeks is likely after a decision to mobilize stockpiled vaccine before the vaccine can be administered to all those wishing to receive it and they have had time to develop protective levels of antibody.
All lots of influenza vaccine sold in Canada must be approved by the health protection branch on a lot by lot basis. No lot will be released unless it meets the high Canadian standards required of all vaccines. I can assure all hon. mem-

bers that there will be no weakening of these standards. The first lots of vaccine were approved for distribution today.

HEALTH-SWINE INFLUENZA-REPORT OF ADVISORY COMMITTEE-REASON FOR DELAY OF MASS IMMUNIZATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you are
aware I have raised twice in this session of parliament important questions concerning the status of mass immunization against swine influenza.
The health authorities at various levels of government, and indeed most Canadians, have an important health decision to make this fall-to vaccinate or not to vaccinate, or to be vaccinated or not be vaccinated. To be specific, one must decide whether to give a vaccination for protection against a possible outbreak caused by the A/New Jersey/76 Virus, better known as swine flu.
The federal government has taken the initiative and given leadership to the provinces in sponsoring an ambitious, bold, and great undertaking in the field of preventive medicine. It is by preventive medicine and health care that the economic burden of illness will be lightened and the tragedy and waste of disease and death reduced.
Influenza has apparently plagued mankind throughout history. However, the great influenza pandemic that swept the world in 1918-19, commonly known as the Spanish flu and today referred to as swine flu, killed 20 million persons, outnumbering World War 1 fatalities by more than two to one.
In February, 1976, a new strain of human influenza virus identified as A/New Jersey/76 and called the swine flu virus was isolated in a few outbreaks among U.S.A. army recruits at Fort Dix, New Jersey. This virus infected about 500 people and took the life of one recruit. Moreover, the outbreak at Fort Dix was a mixed outbreak of swine flu and A-Victoria-3-75 viruses.
On previous occasions when a new major antigenic variant of influenza A virus has been recognized in the human population it has subsequently given rise to a world-wide epidemic. From past experience and present knowledge, it was only prudent to develop a mass vaccination program to protect Canadians against the new strain of influenza virus, especially since the World Health Organization on April 8, 1976, had issued a world-wide alert against a possible swine flu outbreak and urged national health ministries to prepare contingency plans. This program is not without its problems and critics, but action must be taken and problems explained after proper consultation, or else confusion, doubt, and damage to health might follow. Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak briefly on Bill C-15 and wish to place special emphasis on the effect on Canadian agriculture of the operation of the customs tariff, a theme developed by previous speakers.
I am concerned about the methods with which we implement tariffs of a temporary nature, that is, increase duties on certain commodities in order to meet an emergency in Canadian agriculture. At present, I submit our system is too cumbersome. Approval for an increase in tariffs necessary to protect a Canadian farm crop is too long in coming. As always, it is too little and too late. It is too late to protect Canadian agriculture. This applies especially to the Canadian farmer producing fruit and vegetables.
In spring and early summer, when our home-grown produce comes on the market, similar produce from the United States and Mexico still flows into this country and destroys the market for our own farmers. At any rate such foreign produce undermines the market for the first crop harvested by Canadian farmers in the spring. Protection is too little, and comes too late.
Present policies have a disastrous effect on Canadian farmers. They destroy the farmers' will to compete and produce food in Canada. What I mean is perhaps best illustrated by the fact that it took the government a long time to curb the importation of Oceanic beef. I will not go into the subject in detail, since it has already been elaborated on, but it took the government two or three years to enforce, not a tariff but a quota. I say this to show how long it takes the government to act in a time of difficulty for agriculture.
I respectfully suggest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), or senior officials of his department, should have some input with respect to any decision to impose temporary tariffs for the protection of agriculture. Right now our procedures before the Tariff Board take too long.
Let us examine the effect of tariffs on sWe Canadian products to illustrate the irreparable damage which has been done in many cases. As hon. members know, I come from an
(Mr. McKenzie.]
area which produces tobacco. In the tobacco industry we employ strippers-that term has been used several times recently. It carries no moral connotation. Strippers are merely people who strip the leaf from the tobacco after it has been cured. In the last few years the importation of leaf tobacco into Canada has increased by some 1,086 per cent. This has been happening at the same time as Canadian farmers have been producing the same quality of tobacco, at prices just as attractive. The Ontario flu-cured marketing board cannot understand how the government can permit the importation of leaf tobacco which competes directly with our own tobacco in our own markets.
It is true that there is now in place a specific duty of 15 cents a pound on leaf tobacco coming into Canada. That was of some use a number of years ago when tobacco sold at 30 to 40 cents a pound. Now it is selling at 90 cents to $1 a pound. Therefore 15 cents is not much of a barrier against the importation of leaf tobacco.
The effect on the tobacco farmer is simple. We have been forced to cut our production by 50 per cent. This represents a drop in income to the Canadian tobacco farmer of about 50 per cent. When you look at the effect of the whole economy in the tobacco growing area, it becomes serious. I also remind the government that the total take in excise tax, both federal and provincial, is well over $1 billion. Therefore the federal government and governments at all levels should do something to protect this industry which is so lucrative for the Department of National Revenue.
Let us look at the lack of protection for the apple growing industry. The County of Norfolk is noted for its apples. I always compete with the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Whittaker) and the B.C. apples. In any event, we grow pretty good apples in Norfolk County.
The apple growers have been under duress caused by a dumping of apple products. I refer specifically to the dumping of apple concentrate by Italy a year or two ago. With the addition of a little water you had reconstituted apple juice which was sold all across Canada in direct competition with that which is produced here. This was also mentioned by my colleague, the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain). The apple grower is certainly drastically affected by poor management of our tariff structure.
In the same vein a similar type of competition was experienced by tomato growers who supply canning factories in Ontario and, in fact, throughout Canada. The health of that industry has been severely damaged. Tomato paste has been imported from Mexico which is easily reconstituted into catsup, tomato juice, and other such products. We are not afforded protection. As everyone knows, there is an abundance of cheap labour in Mexico.
There is no need for a permanent tariff. We simply have to make an application of a tariff to give our Canadian producers fair competition with imported products, nothing that will damage our relationship as signatories to the GATT agree-

It is very easy to set out some great pattern of world trade and demand the elimination of tariff barriers for commodities and manufactured or semi-manufactured goods, but it is very difficult in a country like this to go to the people with such a suggestion. I have talked to groups in my constituency who are very conscious of the problems in other parts of the world. They tell me they are willing to lower their standard of living in order to help those other countries. That is a problem 1 wrestled with for a while, Mr. Speaker. I admired that spirit, but it seemed to me that if there are individuals in the country who are willing to lower their standard of living for the sake of others, they can. There are many non-governmental agencies to which one can make donations or give some assistance or aid in order to develop other parts of the world. Because we have the kind of democratic system that promises opportunity to its people, I doubt whether it is possible to go to the people and say that we are initiating a trade policy which is going to reduce the standard of living of Canadians.
I think one of the problems of the world is that too few nations are moving toward the kind of democratic system that gives people a real choice in the kind of government they have, and in the policies of the government. If the situation were otherwise, and if democracy seemed to be spreading throughout the world, then we would have more cause to be optimistic about the world trading picture.
I feel we will need a tariff policy for many years to come and that no country can yet afford to destroy its own industries in the hope that this will somehow benefit other parts of the world. If we destroy our agriculture we will not strengthen Chad, Somalianor Mali, but we would certainly give a great boost to the Common Market and our neighbour to the south. Those areas would then be much freer to trade in the world.
When we are competing with countries at least as sophisticated and in many cases more industrialized than Canada we must be cautious and make sure that our agriculture can compete. There is not much point in having lovely rural areas if they are deserted and unproductive. The food shortage will catch up to the world, and I am sure we will be called upon to play a far more important role in feeding the world than at present. It would be a grave mistake if we were to allow agriculture in this country to decline to the point where we could no longer play that role.
This concludes what I want to say on the subject of customs tariff although I have not touched on areas like manufactured goods and a variety of other things. We must be very conscious of the primary industry of this country, however. I represent a constituency in a province where most of the primary industries are in trouble-lumber, agriculture, tourism. Coal mining is the one bright spot but even that has had some unfortunate strikes, partly brought about by inequities in this government's anti-inflation program. It might be possible to be cheerful and optimistic if only one primary industry were in trouble, but when the trouble affects almost all of the primary industries then the province and, I suggest, the country are in a dangerous situation indeed.
I suppose to many poorer nations of the world Canada appears safe, secure, solid and substantial. But I know that many businesses, many industries, are merely hanging on. Their ability to remain in operation and provide employment to Canadians depends on this bill. I ask the minister to review and consider carefully some parts of it because we cannot afford to lose more; particularly in agriculture we cannot afford to lose more than we have already lost.

Perhaps the terminology is poor but the north represents the developed countries and the south the underdeveloped countries. Simultaneously the American tariffs on many goods, as well as their more sophisticated manufacturing sector based upon economies of scale related to larger markets, their greater technology and access to finance, all hindered our development. An additional sore point with some people in Atlantic Canada is that many home grown family and partnership farms and businesses, both in primary and secondary manufacturing, were bought out by larger corporations which often proceeded to close them and supply the maritimes from their central Canadian factories or plants. In doing so they were unimpeded by any federal attempt to intervene, as for example, by a fiscal tool such as a high capital gains tax for selling maritime-owned businesses in order to keep these industries' jobs in the maritime provinces.
Having made that brief, if simplistic, historical incursion into our economic history, and while I do believe the world we are moving into in the 1980's and 1990's is going to be one which will demand greater liberalization of trade between countries, and while believing that Canada has to take a lead in promoting the lowering of tariffs, I must express a caveat.
The free trade model recently proposed by the Economic Council of Canada as a policy option for Canada during the latter half of the 1970's is, in my opinion, a dubious proposition. The modern extensions of Ricardo's model are predicated on an institutional framework that bears little resemblance to the existing international political economic order.
For success, the free trade model requires a laissez faire political and economic system, that is, passive government, truly competitive markets, small, powerless and passive trading firms, unimpeded flows of labour between countries and within national boundaries, free flows of capital and non-managed, flexible exchange rates-no dirty floats. Only when these institutional conditions are met will all the participants in international trade experience any improvements in their real standards of living.
Within the framework of our own confederation we have had free trade, indeed an economic union, between the provinces, but the Atlantic provinces have still suffered. Likewise if you look at the divisions between the rich and the poor sections in Italy, we can agree that free trade even within a country is sometimes injurious to one section of it, or at least plays little role in closing the employment and income gap between national regions. I also believe, and more so after listening to Prime Minister Manley of Jamaica today, that we in the better off countries have to open our markets in a preferential way to Third World countries.
Some would argue that we have a comparative advantage that should be exploited in high technology industries. Indeed a perusal of Canada's trade figures reveals that the country may not even possess a comparative, that is a relative, advan-

tage in high technology industries. Moreover, not only have the high technology manufacturing industries, with few exceptions, performed poorly in foreign markets, but they have also been slipping in the domestic market. Thus it would appear that the strength of Canada's trade advantage resides in the resource sector, a sector that would not likely experience large gains because of free trade. As a result the movement to free trade would, it seems to me, reinforce the Canadian image of hewers of wood and drawers of water.
Obviously in the short run per capita incomes have increased through development of our natural resources and staple products, but we have paid a high price for it. We must now intelligently and vigorously pursue a policy of increased processing of Canada's natural resources, but this move would be inconsistent with free trade in the textbook sense. Furthermore, the regional repercussions of the closing out of a substantial segment of the manufacturing sector-for example, textiles in Quebec-are even more serious than I have indicated.
A substantial decline in employment in the manufacturing sector, compensated by a sharp increase in the share of aggregate employment accounted for by the service sector, could result in a marked deterioration in the productivity potential of the economy. Indeed it is possible that the initial productivity bonus stemming from specialization could be completely offset within four to six years by a lower trend growth in over-all productivity.
Up to now we have assumed that the transition which would occur in the industrial structure as a result of the move toward free trade would be orderly, but the massive industrial restructuring that would be required to maximize the potential benefits from free trade could not in fact take place in an orderly manner, even if we were looking at a relatively long adjustment period. Canada's post-war economic history suggests that this is so for many of our industries that have been protected for a long period.
Moreover, some suggestions that Canada should even go it alone unilaterally in establishing free trade, strike me as being completely unrealistic and could be catastrophic in the consequences of such a step. Canada has to operate Within the context of negotiating under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. At the present time the various countries of the world are engaged in the tedious but important meetings of GATT that are referred to as the Tokyo round of negotiations. It is our belief and hope that a great deal will be accomplished in the liberalization of trade policies for Canada and, indeed, for the world at these meetings.

How would you like to ship a few thousand tons to France? Give it a try some day.
Instead of putting on a reasonable duty through this piece of legislation to protect the grape grower, we are buying surplus grapes in southern Ontario at a cost of something over $1 million. I commend the government for recognizing their financial problem. We will probably do something about processing them and end up spending $330,000.
We will use public funds to subsidize grapes because we have a duty policy which allows concentrates and finished products to come into Canada in competition with our products. The government is dipping into the public purse to correct it. I agree it must dip under the present circumstances. If you were to order wine in government premises anywhere in Ottawa where it might be available, would you get Canadian wine? I wonder whether the grape grower is getting that much support from the Government of Canada, the Minister

of Agriculture, and the Minister of Finance. If I am not mistaken there is a great deal that is foreign and you have to take it without asking.
A classic example of a situation in which there is often a surplus is the potato. The Government of Canada should take note of this example. You cannot get potatoes into the European Economic Community unless there is a drought or shortage to the point of causing great hardship. However, we happen to have a piece of paper which says that following their mid-August decision to suspend the customs external tariff on fresh and chilled cabbage, cauliflower, peas, carrots, celery and potatoes until the end of September, the EEC ministers agreed to prolong this suspension with respect to all these vegetables until the end of the year.
This is one of the very first times that Canada is shipping table stock potatoes into the European Economic Community. They have always had enough of their own and, at times, a surplus. They have not dumped that surplus of potatoes in Canada, but in markets that traditionally belonged to Canada and the United States. They dumped them at prices which scarcely covered the cost of packaging and freight. However, we have no such program.
The Scandinavian countries today say that they are going to ship as many potatoes as they can ship properly, but they are going to protect their consumers and producers by not letting out too many. The ministers of the European Economic Community are going to let some potatoes in, but not too many. They are going to protect their farmers.
Time after time the Australian government has passed regulation after regulation because a particular agricultural commodity was being hurt. We had an extensive market in Australia. However, because a particular Commodity was in competition with a product in Australia, the door was shut forthwith. For some reason or another Canada, as a party to GATT, cannot do the same to anybody else. We can be excluded from markets world-wide without any call for compensation whatsoever. However, when our market is cluttered with dumped produce, no action can be taken because it would contravene our relationship with GATT. It is high time we put ourselves in a different position with GATT.
There are close to a million tons surplus of potatoes on the North American continent, 400,000 pounds of which are in Canada. I hope that the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Agriculture, and the Minister of Finance will co-operate in their search for markets and duty concessions so that the Minister of Agriculture and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) will not again have to dip into the public purse to bail out the potato farmer. I will be brief, Mr. Speaker, because I do not want to kill the legislation introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). Besides, that would be a lack of courtesy on my part if I wanted to kill his bill, and I want to congratulate him for his stubbornness. Every year since I have been in the House of Commons, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has introduced this bill aimed at doing away with that famous old institution-the Senate.
Today, I believe he is just asking for his bill to be referred to the committee for a more thorough study. This is my opinion is very reasonable, for hon. members who have opinions about the Senate could make them known before the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
Mr. Speaker, when we question the people, we get surprising answers. A while ago, I heard someone who probably wants to become a senator try to prove the usefulness of the Senate. I assure you that 98 per cent of the people consider the Senate an absolutely useless institution. I am surprised that the Senate still exists in the federal government because all the provinces have decided that it is a useless institution. The proof of this is that one by one they have all eliminated their second chamber. As someone said earlier, the last province to do so was Quebec. And what fights and discussions there were before this old monument could be eliminated in Quebec! All other Canadian provinces had already done away with their legislative council. People said about Quebecers: Quebec is the most royalist of all the provinces of Canada since it is so attached to its legislative council.
Another reason for my surprise is the fact that the federal government has always more or less shown the way to provinces and that I now realize that it has been given a lesson by all the provinces and that it has not learned from it. Today we are wondering simply what is the usefulness of the Senate. Indeed, all citizens wonder about this. In my opinion, to be fair to the population, we should simply hold a referendum throughout Canada to ask the opinion of the people. Indeed, are we not supposed to reflect the opinion of the people? The government would like to anticipate all the wishes of the big financiers. On the social level, it seems to me that we should be more interested in the opinion of the people.
If by chance this bill were sent to the committee and if a referendum concerning the Senate were suggested, the population could decide if it needs it and if it wishes to keep this old monument. In that case, it would be renovated and kept as other old monuments. But I am convinced, as hon. members all are, that if there were a referendum, 80 per cent of the population would vote to abolish the Senate. This is why I rose in support of the bill introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. In fact, what does being a senator mean? We say it is an honorary title. It is not even an honorary title, Mr. Speaker, it is a dishonorary title because half of the defeated members are appointed there to hide their shame. And it is called an honorary title. Nevertheless, in my opinion an honorary title should be granted to a great scientist.

If a great man stands out in society, such a title would give him the opportunity to perform his scientific work or any other important task for 10 or 12 more years. This is not what we do. Right after his defeat, a member is appointed to the Senate.
That is called an honorary title. What is the population expected to think of such a gesture? If only the members of the Senate were elected, they would at least have a few responsibilities. The House of Commons has all the responsibilities as things are, because its members alone are elected and they are accountable to the people. Because the senator is not elected, he has no responsibility; yet he enjoys all the privileges of those who are elected and who have responsibilities; worse still, he has a right of veto on all the House of Commons does.
Mr. Speaker, the right of veto the Senate has today it did not get from the people. I say those who are truly responsible are those the members of parliament who are elected by the people, who are sent here to work for the people. Moreover, they should not shift their responsibilities on civil servants. Today, there is another type of senator, the civil-servant-senator who does the work of the MPs, who takes over their responsibilities though he is not elected at all.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian people has had enough of these irresponsible groups, of the groups they cannot meet, and who do not care about their opinions. Some people say that senators represent an area, but it is not true. The only thing a senator represents, is his seat in the other place, that's all.
He is like a civil servant. What does he represent? His office, this is all he represents; he has no other responsibility. Those who have the responsibility are those who have been elected by the people. When there are blows, they get them while civil servants laugh at us because they have been given absolute control.
It is about the same with the Senate. They have a right of veto over all our work while the people gave them no authority. We could have an elected Senate, which would be responsible and smaller, as suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), a Senate with 25 or 30 senators. This would be enough; fewer senators would sleep in the Senate, that's all. If we want to keep this monument, let us make it smaller, but at least let us have elected senators and let us have them take responsible actions before the people of Canada. This is ultimately why I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that this bill should be referred to the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs so that at least hon. members can go before the committee and speak about this matter.

I think it is also because I am a friend of the Senate. He could join an ex-colleague. I used to hear a former member for Assiniboia wanting to abolish the Senate two or three times a session. He now sits over there as Senator Hazen Argue. The hon. member would also have other friends. Senator Eugene Forsey not only became a senator but a Liberal. He was not always so. There would be lots of opportunities for him.
Perhaps one of the flaws in our system is that we are occasionally a little casual about improving our rules of procedure. As the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson) has stated, we all know very well that while, strictly speaking, and in terms of the constitution, this second body has an absolute veto, it keeps its position in our structure by not using it, or as Senator Forsey has said, by not acting like madmen or fools. I think it would be wise to reform the Senate by removing that veto or making it applicable for a limited time. To have an absolute veto that they do not use for political reasons strikes me as not being a very good structure. I think some improvement in that regard could be made.
I think the hon. member's bill will not get support. While there are many things we could do to improve the life of the Canadian people, I doubt whether the destruction of the Senate tomorrow would really benefit many Canadians. It would do very little for the people who were disbanded, even if they were pensioned off, as has been suggested.
To write off the long-established Senate of Canada and say it is useless and makes no contribution is, I think, with all due respect, a bit myopic. I know it is a good subject for humour. I remember discussing the dear old chap who was there until he was 104 years of age and who was accused of never having made a speech in his life. That was contradicted. He said he made two speeches, one the day he came there when he denied that his appointment was a result of political corruption, and one on the day when he was congratulated on his 100th birthday. But he always obeyed the bell. It is such a gentle bell over there. It is so different from ours that it almost makes one have longings.
The hon. member has given us an opportunity to debate an old chestnut. I admire his tenacity and respect his views, but I hope his drastic, destructive action will not be supported by this Chamber.

That number, 104, relates to the number of seats allotted to the various provinces as they entered confederation. As a member from western Canada, I feel somewhat relieved that there are 24 senators from western Canada in that chamber. If we ever did get into a bind, they would be there. I hope we shall never get into a situation where they are needed, but I cannot prophesy what will come about in the future. Even the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, with his great wisdom, cannot prophesy the future except, possibly, that he will be here for another 34 years, which might be not so much a prophesy as a statement of fact.
Although I disagree with the hon. member's bill, I hope that some time in the future discussion can be held as to the role of the Senate, so that not only members of this House but the people across Canada will have an opportunity to consider the operations of that body. As things are, very few Canadians really understand its purpose and function.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre probably expresses the views of the majority of Canadians when he states that the Senate should be abolished, not because those who hold such views are basing them on any personal knowledge of the subject; their attitude arises, I suppose, from the failure of the Senate to do a very good job of justifying its existence. Nor have we acknowledged sufficiently the importance of the investigations which the Senate has carried on to help this House in innumerable ways. Senators have been able to do a great deal of work with which we would otherwise be saddled.
These things should be made known to the people of Canada so that they would have some basis upon which to determine the value of the Senate and its place in the constitution. Is it to be regarded as a body of men who merely sit over there in their latter years, waiting for the grim reaper in very comfortable conditions, or is their expertise and experience being used for the benefit of the people of Canada? I have already referred to the aid they give to the House of Commons. Might the abolition of the Senate only create an extended form of bureaucracy brought about by the need to find others to carry on research or committee work?
There might be ways in which the operation of the Senate could be improved. However, let us not, in the words of the old saying, throw the baby out with the bath water. Let us make the Senate a productive body and then give the message to the rest of Canada.

No, they did not. The question of a second Chamber is a serious one. The American founding fathers spent a great deal of time on this matter. Thomas Jefferson used a rather homely metaphor when he was asked, "Why do you need this second Chamber?" He used to pour his tea into a saucer, as was the custom in those days. He saucered the tea into his mouth and said, "It's a little cooler that way".
I was much impressed when I got the chance to visit the great city of Brasilia, with all its interesting and magnificent buildings, and I discovered that their bicameral legislature meets in a building that looks very much like a cup and saucer. It is a very futuristic city; I am not an architect, but that is what it looked like.
I was talking the other day to a very prominent member of the NDP who told me that he had been over to London to visit the Westminster Houses of Parliament. He went into the gallery of the House of Lords and heard there the finest debates he had ever heard dealing in a fundamental, philosophic, yet very practical way with the great problems that the British were facing. Hon. members have no doubt read excerpts from the House of Lords debates which appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail last week. Those are the debates my NDP friend heard.
I believe we should not forget the capacity for infinite improvement. We should have hope enough to think that we can reform. Reform has been in the air for a long time. In 1893 the first political convention in Canada was held in Ottawa. It was not a leadership convention but all of the Liberals who could get to Ottawa came to a great big meeting.

The hon. member has raised a very interesting point, one that many Canadians perhaps consider to be a fault in the way the Senate has been set up, in that it is not an elected House as is the House of Commons. That is the way the Senate was set up originally. We have a great deal of debate in this House by its elected members. If the Senate were an elected House, surely they could speak with power similar to that of the elected representatives in this House. Although it is undemocratic to appoint someone to the Senate in the manner the hon. member spoke of, it would cause a gigantic kerfuffle between the two Houses if both were elected and both had the power of elected members.
Senator Eugene Forsey, commenting on the role of the Senate, said that unless the Senate takes leave of its senses and throws out a bill which a large majority of the people ardently desire, the question of abolition of the Senate will remain purely academic. The Senate knows it does not have enough political clout to do anything of the sort. In other words, the Senate may be undemocratic in the sense that it is not elected, but by the same token it realizes it is part of the process. It knows it does not have enough political clout to override the views and wishes of the House.
On the question of more power for the Senate, Senator Forsey covered this very well when he said that if you gave it more power there would be more power to make a nuisance of it, which is not what it should be. Making it an elected body would certainly do this. He said an elected Senate would claim to be just as representative of public opinion as the elected Commons, and would proceed to throw its weight around.
Many people in Canada do not understand the Senate. They regard it as a rest home for retired politicians-

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND

-a rest home for people who deserve well from the community by reason of their outstanding services. But let us go back in history. As the hon. member said, Sir

John A. Macdonald, when the functions of the Senate were under discussion, said it was a chamber for sober second thought. I have always thought this was an amusing phrase, coming from Sir John A. Macdonald, and I wish I were sure whether he was being facetious or not. The Senate does perform a function in overseeing legislation. I believe the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) would admit that very useful amendments have been brought forward by the Senate with respect to legislation which had passed through the Commons.

But this is not the only important function of the Senate. A number of very useful reports have been made by that body or its committees. I think in particular of the study on poverty in Canada carried out under the chairmanship of Senator Croll. I believe the hon. member would agree that a great many members of the Senate have distinguished themselves in business and private life. Many of them have acquired great experience in municipal affairs, as provincial politicians and as politicians at the federal level. This knowledge and experience shows itself in reports such as the one to which I have referred.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre glossed over the fact that the Senate was brought into being for a specific purpose. The maritime provinces and Quebec felt there had to be a chamber where representation was not based simply upon numbers of population. It was evident even in those days that the population of the Maritimes was not likely to be substantial compared with, say, that of Ontario. In the early days of confederation it was feared in Quebec that the population might be greatly exceeded by that of Ontario, and that the strength of the representation in the Commons would be greatly diminished if the population of Ontario rose disproportionately. For this reason a proposal was adopted which ensured the presence of a guaranteed number of senators from Quebec, supposedly to look after the interests of that province.
Mr. Speaker, the Maritimes' population certainly has not increased proportionately with the rest of Canada. The hon. member tells us there is no longer much concern about the need for regional representation based on population. I am not so sure. I do not know anyone who can guarantee that the situation which the builders of our institution had in mind so long ago could not arrive, at a point in our history, where strong regional interest was involved, perhaps in the Prairies, perhaps in the Maritimes. When Quebec, the Maritimes and Ontario entered confederation they were allotted 24 representatives. The basis upon which these, seats were allocated remains unchanged to this day.
The hon. member says that 104 people seated in the Senate is too many; that their maintenance is too heavy a burden for the taxpayers of Canada to pay. But as I understand him, he is not directing his criticism to numbers. What he is saying is, abolish the Senate whether it is 104, 50, 25 or 5.

True, it was prepared before he had any notion that he might be summoned to that other place. In that memorandum he said that the Senate of Canada is the most undemocratic institution in the world. He went on to point out that it has unlimited veto power; it can say "no" to a decision of the House of Commons not just once or 100 times, but a thousand times. He said it in typical Forsey language, and I think he was right. The Senate as we have it in this country is as undemocratic as it can possibly be. Senator Forsey did not mean, and I do not mean, that the persons now in the Senate are undemocratic in their approach to things. What we are talking about is the structure, the constitutional provision which allows the will of the elected people to be overridden by those in the other place.
Sometimes persons who discuss this question with me say, "But you fellows in the House of Commons make mistakes now and then; it is good to have somebody else giving those matters sober second thought." It is a plausible argument; but by what right do those individuals in the other place have the authority to reject what we do? I point out that some in the other place have tried to get in here, into this House. Perhaps they ran for re-election and were defeated. In other words, the public said they did not want those persons in the Parliament of Canada, but they got in through the back door.
I suggest, also, that there are many more conflicts of interest in the other place than have been identified in this place. I think it is particularly unfortunate that matters involving banks, financial institutions and company incorporations are dealt with in that body which has the same authority as we have but which includes many persons with an interest in a number of those institutions.
It is sometimes argued that there are good persons over there, men and women who do good work on committees. They do. Some of their committee reports have been quite useful. They have gone into their subjects very thoroughly. However, I do not see why we should maintain 104 persons on the full pay that goes with being a senator and all the pension benefits that are down the road so that 15 or 20 can do good committee work. There are many professors, academics, businessmen, trade unionists and other people around the country who can be seconded for the kind of committee work that needs to be done. As I say, maintaining 104 for the work that 25 or 30 of them will do is surely not common sense.
I do not see the argument for reform that persons sometimes put forward. In fact, it often happens in the debate that takes place on this bill of mine. Some members will say that this member goes too far, that there are things wrong with the Senate, but let us reform it. Once in a while they start a debate on Senate reform in the other place, but they never finish it. The only reform that seems to have any logic is to provide for the senators to be elected in some way. If we were to do that, if we were to give them the moral authority of being responsible to the electorate, we would add to the stresses and strains of government in this country to no end. We have enough dif-

ficulty now in the conflict between the executive and parliament and between the parliament of Canada and the various legislatures without adding another conflict of two Houses with equal authority in terms of their being elected. I think the best answer is to look at the possibility of a unicameral parliament, namely, one House which can be responsible to the people of this country and do this nation's business.
At one time in our history several of our provinces had an upper chamber, but they were done away with one by one. The last one was that in the province of Quebec. How did they get rid of them? In some cases they pensioned off those who were there. That might seem to cost something at the moment, but the cost would be quite minimal compared with what it costs to maintain the Senate in perpetuity. Another argument that is sometimes used is that we have always had it, and therefore we should keep it. That argument keeps us doing a lot of things. I have had members around here ask me about certain reforms that ought to be made in this place. I sometimes have to say I have been through that half a dozen times over the last few decades. It just seems to have been around here for some time and that is why we keep it. That is no argument for the Senate.
It has been argued that the Senate is a place of sober second thought. The people who do the sober second thinking about what goes on here are the people of Canada, not some individuals who, as I have already said, are responsible to no one. There are those who still trot out the argument that in some way the Senate protects minorities. Sir, it does not protect anything. Certainly it does not protect minorities. Minorities are protected in this House where we are responsible to the various groups in the country. The other place where minority rights are protected is the courts.
All told, the case is a good one for revising what the Fathers of Confederation came up with 109 or 110 years ago, and doing away with the other place. My bill proposes this. It is very precise as to the changes that should be made to the constitution. It even has in it a precise date when it should come into effect, namely, July 1, 1977. In other words, Their Honours can have another seven or eight months. I know that the possibility of that happening is not great. However, I do think it is a serious question which we ought to be discussing in these days when we are concerned about the structure and nature of the Parliament of Canada.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that this bill which proposes the abolition of the Senate will at least receive the approval of this House this afternoon, so that it can be sent for study to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

He said: Mr. Speaker, if members of the House were prepared to proceed immediately to a vote on this matter I would, of course, withhold my speech, but it has been indicated to me that there are one or two who have views other than mine.
Sir, the purpose of this bill is quite clear. It would, among other things, change section 17 of our constitution, the British North America Act, to make it read:
There shall be One Parliament for Canada, consisting of the Queen and the House of Commons.
In other words, the clear purpose of this bill is to abolish the Senate. I am sure this bill does not come as a surprise to hon. members. I have not counted the number of times I have introduced it. Before I drafted the actual bill I used to bring in motions and resolutions of one kind and another; therefore, 1 suppose it can be said that since the time I came here I have been arguing for the abolition of the other place.
Someone said to me a while ago that I was not being very effective, that I had been arguing for the abolition of the Senate for 34 years and it is still there. I replied that perhaps I had almost succeeded. Out of all the members who were over there when I first came here and called for the abolition of the Senate, only three remain. So in one way or another we have got rid of most of them. The job is almost done. True, there are quite a number of vacancies in the other place. Perhaps they could just be left. Those vacancies could act as a sort of carrot to induce certain persons to behave, but perhaps we could get rid of the other place in that way.
Seriously, Mr. Speaker, I hope that some day-and I do not see why this should not be the day-the House will at least let this bill go to the appropriate standing committee for discussion of this matter. Not all members of the House agree that
BN A Act
the Senate ought to be abolished. But surely in these days when questions are being asked about parliament, democracy and democratic institutions, it is a reasonable proposition that we, in the elected House of this parliament, should look at the provision of 1867 for another place and decide if that place should continue. It is my strong view that it should not.
When I ask that the bill be sent to the appropriate committee, I admit that there are arguments both ways. In fact, there are so many arguments and there is so much to say that we can hardly make a decision in the space of one private members' hour. That is why I plead seriously with the House. I submit that instead of talking this proposition out, the House should allow it to go, either as a bill or as the subject matter thereof, to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs for study by members of that committee.
Although I said there are arguments on both sides, and I do recognize that, so far as I am concerned all the arguments are on one side. I believe in democracy. I believe in this country being governed by the people and I think we have devised the right way for being governed by the people, namely, government by elected representatives who pass the laws and discuss the issues which concern a land such as ours.
Perhaps 109 or 110 years ago it seemed appropriate, in a day when the House of Lords was an important institution in the United Kingdom, that we in this country should also have a second body to look at what is done by elected representatives in this chamber. Surely Canada has grown up. Surely democracy has grown to the point where there is no case for the proposition that a group of men and women responsible to no one should have veto power over what is decided by those who have been elected by the people of this country. I emphasize that once a person is appointed to the Senate he is responsible to no one, not even to the prime minister who named him. He is there until age 75. Some of the members in the other place were appointed when the time limit was life itself. They are living out their appointments.
The concept of a democracy which does not go all the way does not, in my view, fit into our thinking today. If we believe that the people have been right to enjoy responsible government, the only persons who should have a say in the making of our laws should be those who are responsible back to the electorate, the people of Canada. I am not suggesting that all the things the Senate does are wrong and all the things this House does are right. I am not suggesting that mistakes are not made in this place. But, sir, every three, four or five years we have to go back to the electorate, back to the people of Canada for their verdict as to whether we should carry on. At the same time, we have this archaic set-up in which a group of 104 men and women-assuming all the places are filled-have the unquestioned right to veto and defeat any decisions made in the House of Commons, and they do not have to answer to anyone. To me that set-up is as undemocratic as it can be.
I am not the only one who makes extreme statements of that kind. I have in my possession, although I do not have it with me at the moment, a memorandum on the Senate which was prepared a number of years ago by Senator Eugene Forsey.

This unfavourable price spread persisted throughout the balance of 1975, and worsened in 1976. By April, 1976, Canada was allowing beef to be imported at 16 cents to 17 cents per pound cheaper than beef of identical quality being shipped to the United States. In May, 1976, offshore imports of beef and veal were running 40 per cent ahead of 1975 levels, and by October imports had increased by 60 per cent over the previous year.
This government has the audacity to go around the country claiming that the Anti-Inflation Act is working because food prices have decreased, yet it fails to recognize that anyone who has entered the fourth year of the beef marketing system is selling livestock below the cost of production. I have sympathy for anyone who has to buy a basket of food today. One of this country's objectives should be to produce food as cheaply as possible. That cannot happen as long as the kind of long-range policy we have drives people out of production. We are faced with depressed prices in Canada. Canadian cattlemen will almost certainly be forced to greatly reduce their herds, and in the long run we will have either lost a major producing industry, we will pay higher prices for meat, or even import almost all our meat.
On June 11 Canada imposed what has become known as the infamous six-cent under rule whereby the government unnecessarily made an agreement that oceanic beef cannot be sold in Canada at a price discount greater than six cents under identical quality beef being sold in the United States. This forced Canadian beef prices to floor levels, and will continue to do so as long as the rule is in force. The obvious result is that the government's action has dangerously eroded our trading relationships in beef and veal with the United States. Anyone who has had the experience in recent months of talking to farmers and ranchers in the United States will recognize that this has a very serious and detrimental effect on our traditional trading pattern of two-way trade with the United States.
I think it is very important to underscore the difference between Canada's trade with the United States and that of the oceanic countries. The first difference in our trade with the United States is that it is a two-way trade; not only does Canada export to the United States but we also import. The two countries are producing at about equal cost and have an almost equal standard of living. There is quite a difference when you compare that with oceanic beef with regard to which almost every other beef producing country has established a

As an indication of how serious this situation is, let me say, Mr. Speaker, that ranchers today are gathering at meetings all across the country to protest the actions of this government. Nothing can underscore their concern more than the fact that 300 people gathered in Lethbridge two days ago on two days' notice. Mr. Speaker, I repeat that 300 ranchers gathered on two days' notice to voice their concern about what is happening to this country's producers. In my province, Alberta, virtually every day meetings are held in local auction marts and community halls. Ranchers are protesting. They want to know what they can do. They know they are about to lose their farming and ranching businesses if the government's present import quotas are not changed. In my constituency a meeting was held on October 22. Eight hundred ranchers showed up from across Alberta, parts of British Columbia and parts of Saskatchewan to learn what was happening in the marketing of beef and veal.
There is great concern on the part of ranchers because exports from New Zealand increased by 139 per cent this year, and from Australia by 10 per cent. Mr. Speaker, we have literally become a dumping ground for cheap meat so that the Prime Minister can tell the people of Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and southern Ontario that the anti-inflation program is working. He tries to demonstrate the truth of his assertion by saying, "Last year your food bill rose 10 per cent. This year it has risen only 6.2 per cent." The number of items which have actually decreased in price is small. You will find that one such decrease has occurred in a product which the government has allowed to be imported into this country in order to keep food costs down. I am referring to meat. While it is creditable to attempt to keep food prices down, it is not creditable to try to aid one part of the country at the expense of another. That is what is malicious about the present government's actions.
Let us consider some of the facts laid before the House on Tuesday by the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Whittaker). He said, as reported on page 472 of Hansard, that Canada has a cheap food policy, something the producer regions of this country know. Mr. Speaker, it is apparent that the government considers those in the producer regions as politically expendable. It does all it can to provide cheap food, despite the injustice such a policy may occasion to a certain part of the country. For example, in 1975 this country imported 83 per cent more dairy foods than in 1973. We imported 370 per cent more berries than in 1973, 58 per cent more apples, 200 per cent more honey, 74 per cent more jams, 294 per cent more chicken, and 33 per cent more canned ham.
In 1974 Canada imported 5 million pounds of chicken from the United States. Figures up to June of 1976 show that Canada imported 22 million pounds of chicken from the United States, or 400 per cent more than in 1975. Small wonder that Canada seems to be eroding at the seams or

The truth of the matter is that any cheap food we have in this country is here because we have imported it at considerably cheaper rates, and in the process of doing that we are literally destroying whole regions of Canada and the production which takes place in those regions. What is happening is that the sense of power of this government has caused it to feel that it can write off an area of Canada.
In terms of seats, the Liberal government does not have much power from the prairies, so it feels it can write off the prairies. The government knows that there are more members from Montreal and Toronto than there are from all three prairie provinces combined, so it imposes an import quota which allows this country to bring in cheap food. To some extent I sympathize with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) because I realize the bind he is in within the cabinet. In response to a question asked yesterday by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) with reference to the 6-cent under clause on frozen meat from Australia and New Zealand, the minister responded by saying that new negotiations will take place. He said he hopes the result will be that meat shipped to Canada will be sold at a price no different from the price of meat shipped to the United States under the quota system which has been imposed.
It is interesting to note that when he was speaking to the Cattlemen's Association here just two days ago, it was admitted by one of the top economic authorities of the Department of Agriculture that the department had never favoured the 6-cent under clause. The truth of the matter is that the minister obviously lost out in cabinet. Perhaps with good intentions the minister was trying to protect our agricultural industry, but so it would appear that the AIB was working, farmers, ranchers and producers of apples and other products were simply sold down the river.
Since 1969 Canada has imported about 7 per cent of its domestic consumption of boneless beef. Traditionally, these imports were of low quality and did not compete directly with Canadian products. After 1974, however, following a period in which the government encouraged ranchers to increase herd
[Mr. Malone.)
sizes, there was a growing importation of medium and high quality beef in direct competition with domestic production. The nature of that activity placed us in direct conflict with our traditional trading partners, namely, the United States of America.
Because of lack of policy in respect of quotas of meat coming in from other countries, Canada has become almost an enemy of the United States in the area of trade in meat. Anyone who talks to the producers, farmers and ranchers of the United States knows they are angry at Canada for dumping meat on a run-through from oceanic countries to Canada and then forcing the meat of Canada to be dumped into the United States. Canada, a country that has the capacity to produce enough domestic beef to meet its requirements, is the only nation in the world with no controls over the quantity of imports. All other major beef producing nations impose effective import controls. I think it is absolutely shocking that Canada, as a major meat producing country, is the only country without import controls.
Let us look at some examples, Mr. Speaker. The United States, the world's largest importer of beef, imports nearly 30 per cent of the beef and veal in world trade channels; however, the United States has laws that limit imports to 7 per cent of domestic consumption. If we look at the United Kingdom and the European Economic Community, we note that this group represents the second largest importer of the world's beef. The imports are very closely controlled, however, by means of a complex system of fixed duties, variable levies, ad valorem duties and quotas. In July, 1974, the European Economic Community banned beef and veal imports by way of embargo. Japan is now a major importer of world beef, ranking third behind the European Economic Community and the United States, yet Japan exercises control over imports through state buying agencies, a 25 per cent ad valorem tariff, variable levies and quota allocations. Early in 1974 Japan virtually placed embargoes on all imports of beef and veal until September, 1975.
In 1975 and 1976 Canada literally became a dumping ground for the world's beef and veal surpluses, a situation to which no other country has to date been exposed. I think it is despicable that this government goes around the country praising its anti-inflation program, saying that the AIB is working, when it is driving almost 100,000 farmers and ranchers in this country into a loss situation. The Minister of Finance, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien), and the Minister of Agriculture have to bear responsibility for the 100,000 people who are now entering their fourth year of selling livestock at below the cost of production.
In spite of our small population, Canada now ranks the fourth largest importer of beef in world trade channels. In 1976 Canada ranked first on beef imports, on a per capita basis. Here is a country with the capacity to produce all the beef we need for domestic consumption, yet we are the fourth largest importer of beef in the world. This makes a sham of the government's policies, and Bill C-15 fails to pay any attention to this situation. One of the obvious injustices of Bill C-15 is

I should like, first of all, to demonstrate that much of what is being changed in our Customs Tariff Act has been taking place in an attempt to promote political ambitions in Canada.
I believe it is important as a background that we begin to realize that agriculture has been a very important aspect of all cultures and civilizations. No culture has ever advanced without a deep-rooted respect for, and easy access to, agriculture and agricultural products. But once industrialized, this nation tended to treat agriculture with cynical disregard.
The Canadian food producers have been the victims of a malicious ploy by the Liberal government, not as the national government but toward the central regionalization of this country. In desperation, to patch up its own economic mismanagement it has divided Canada for selfish, political reward. The facts are that there are more members of parliament in the city of Toronto than in the whole of the province of Alberta. Moreover, there are more members of parliament from Toronto and Montreal than there are in the three prairie provinces. That all links together with the Customs Tariff Act when we note that 78 per cent of the beef production in Canada comes from the three prairie provinces, and most of it from the province of Alberta.
With 19 Conservative seats in the province of Alberta, this government, filled with the venom of politics, has decided to sacrifice one region of this country for the glut of continuing in political power. The government claims that the anti-inflation program is working because food costs are down. The truth of the matter is that food costs in this country are not down, and any comment in that regard is simply a fabrication of the facts. The truth is that food costs in Canada are up. What is happening is that the government of today is importing into this country cheap food from countries which produce food at less cost, to give the appearance that food costs generally are down. In other words the government of Canada is sacrificing the producers of this country for the consumers. The only reason food prices appear to be down is the callous and calculated attempt by the government to willingly destroy the livelihood of 100,000 beef producers by the import and export quota regulations for the selfish reason of trying to prove the Anti-Inflation Board is working.
I should like to point out that the situation has become so desperate as to cause grave concern and problems among the producers of this nation. Imports of pork have risen dramatically in recent years since 1973 when we imported into Canada 215 million pounds. In 1975 we imported 453 million pounds, or an increase of 110 per cent. In October of 1976 we increased our imports by another 82 per cent over 1975. It must be noted that at the same time our exports of pork are down 7 per cent.
The point I am trying to make is quite simple. The government of the day is of the opinion that it must justify the anti-inflation program to the Canadian public, and in a malicious and calculating way is attempting, at the expense of the producers, to prove that the anti-inflation program is working.

I have in hand a collection of speeches and policy statements made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and cabinet ministers. The material is quite weighty and bulky. It is an attempt to demonstrate what the government is saying across the country, namely, that the anti-inflation program is working and the proof of it is that food prices are down.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR DISCLOSURE OF DECENTRALIZATION PLAN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the President of the Treasury Board. 1 should like to preface it by expressing the pleasure of my party at the fact that the government is acting on decentralization of the functions of the public service in the country. I would like the minister to confirm that there will be a major policy announcement regarding the Department of Veterans Affairs and public servants employed by that department made outside this House immediately after question period ends today.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (President of the Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR DISCLOSURE OF DECENTRALIZATION PLAN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that question should more properly be addressed to my colleague, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR DISCLOSURE OF DECENTRALIZATION PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am still responsible for the federal government decentralization program, and I am glad to see that the Leader of the Opposition maintains the stand he had himself included in his program. I hope he will speak to his neighbour right across from me and to his other neighbour as well, for I am sure the member for Saint-Hyacinthe agrees with that decentralization policy. This afternoon, the Minister of Veterans Affairs is to make a statement in Charlottetown because I think this is the most appropriate place to make it at this time, since this is a place which really needs the help of the federal government.
As to the policy itself, I have already made statements and speeches about it in the House. If anybody wants me to make another statement, Mr. Speaker, I will be glad to do so, and I would then quote statements of policy the member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark) made when he ran for the leadership of his party.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF STAFF REDUCTIONS IN ATLANTIC REGION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43 I rise on a matter of extreme urgency and pressing necessity so far as the employees of the Canadian National in the Atlantic region are concerned.
In view of the fact that the CN is continuing a policy of cut-backs and lay-offs of their employees, affecting trainmen, engineers, telegraphers, CN police, customer relations officers and CN-CP Telecommunication employees with many years of service without due and timely, or indeed decent notice, causing great hardship to these employees and their families, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Cumberland-Colches-ter North:
That the Minister of Transport cause an immediate investigation to be carried out into the operations of the Canadian National Railways in the Atlantic region to determine why these employees with so many years service are being treated in such a cruel and callous manner by this Crown corporation when, at the same time, the throne speech pays lip service to job creation in regions of chronic unemployment.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL CANADA REQUEST UNITED STATES TO STOP CONSTRUCTION OF GARRISON DIVERSION UNTIL INTERNATIONAL JOINT COMMISSION REPORTS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the fact that the International Joint Commission has been granted an extension to June 1977 to complete its report on the Garrison Diversion Project of North Dakota, and recognizing that $23.5 million for next year's construction has already been appropriated by Congress, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp):
That the House direct the Prime Minister to request the government of the United States to immediately stop all construction of the Garrison diversion until the International Joint Commission has completed and presented its final report.
